```{r setup, include = FALSE}
# Renders the handout from the estimates of handout_preferred_specification.R
# (run it first). Equations are written in LaTeX and become native, editable
# Word equations; tables are native Word tables (flextable).
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, dpi = 200)
library(flextable)
library(ggplot2)
e <- readRDS(file.path("results", "handout_preferred_specification", "estimates.rds"))
# PWT against World Bank GDP and the outliers (handout_sources.R).
src <- readRDS(file.path("results", "handout_preferred_specification", "sources.rds"))
set_flextable_defaults(font.family = "Calibri", font.size = 8, padding = 1.5)
ybar <- exp(e$inc_mean)
pp <- function(x, d = 2) formatC(100 * x, format = "f", digits = d)
pv <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.001, "< 0.001", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))
stars <- function(p) ifelse(p < 0.01, "***", ifelse(p < 0.05, "**", ifelse(p < 0.1, "*", "")))
fit <- e$fit
g <- e$grid
xi_p <- function(x) g$p_score[abs(g$xi - x) < 1e-9]
aic_of <- function(x) g$aic[abs(g$xi - x) < 1e-9]

# Readable row labels of the terms, in the order of the tables (each arm
# followed by its interactions).
TERM_LABELS <- c(
  dTM = "T deviation d_T (symmetric)", "dTM:clim_TM" = "   T deviation × climate c_T",
  pTM = "T warm arm D⁺_T", "pTM:clim_TM" = "   warm × climate c_T", "pTM:y" = "   warm × income y",
  "pTM:agr" = "   warm × agr. share s",
  nTM = "T cold arm D⁻_T", "nTM:clim_TM" = "   cold × climate c_T", "nTM:y" = "   cold × income y",
  "nTM:agr" = "   cold × agr. share s",
  "pTM:r" = "T warm arm D⁺_T × (Ȳ/Y)^(1−ξ)", "pTM:clim_TM:r" = "   warm × climate c_T × (Ȳ/Y)^(1−ξ)",
  "nTM:r" = "T cold arm D⁻_T × (Ȳ/Y)^(1−ξ)", "nTM:clim_TM:r" = "   cold × climate c_T × (Ȳ/Y)^(1−ξ)",
  dRR = "P deviation d_P (symmetric)", "dRR:clim_RR" = "   P deviation × climate c_P",
  pRR = "P wet arm D⁺_P", "pRR:clim_RR" = "   wet × climate c_P", "pRR:y" = "   wet × income y",
  "pRR:agr" = "   wet × agr. share s",
  nRR = "P dry arm D⁻_P", "nRR:clim_RR" = "   dry × climate c_P", "nRR:y" = "   dry × income y",
  "nRR:agr" = "   dry × agr. share s",
  "pTM2:r" = "T warm arm squared (D⁺_T)² × (Ȳ/Y)^(1−ξ)", "pTM2:clim_TM:r" = "   warm² × climate c_T × (Ȳ/Y)^(1−ξ)",
  "nTM2:r" = "T cold arm squared (D⁻_T)² × (Ȳ/Y)^(1−ξ)", "nTM2:clim_TM:r" = "   cold² × climate c_T × (Ȳ/Y)^(1−ξ)",
  pRR2 = "P wet arm squared (D⁺_P)²", "pRR2:clim_RR" = "   wet² × climate c_P", "pRR2:agr" = "   wet² × agr. share s",
  nRR2 = "P dry arm squared (D⁻_P)²", "nRR2:clim_RR" = "   dry² × climate c_P", "nRR2:agr" = "   dry² × agr. share s",
  clim_TM = "Level: climate c_T", clim_RR = "Level: climate c_P", y = "Level: income y"
)
pr <- readRDS(file.path("results", "handout_preferred_specification", "projections.rds"))
library(sf)
# A coefficient table of models `ms` (names: column headers): estimate (pp)
# with stars, clustered SE below, then the fit.
coef_table <- function(ms, coefs = e$coefs, fits = NULL) {
  terms <- unique(unlist(lapply(coefs[ms], `[[`, "term")))
  terms <- terms[order(match(terms, names(TERM_LABELS)))]
  cols <- lapply(ms, function(k) {
    x <- coefs[[k]]
    i <- match(terms, x$term)
    ifelse(is.na(i), "", paste0(pp(x$estimate[i], 3), stars(x$p[i]), "\n(", pp(x$se[i], 3), ")"))
  })
  out <- data.frame(Term = unname(TERM_LABELS[terms]), cols, check.names = FALSE)
  names(out)[-1] <- names(ms)
  if (!is.null(fits)) {
    extra <- data.frame(Term = c("Observations (countries)", "AIC", "BIC", "Within adj. R²"),
                        do.call(cbind, lapply(fits, function(f) c(sprintf("%s (%d)", format(f$rows, big.mark = ","), f$countries),
                                                                  sprintf("%.1f", f$aic), sprintf("%.1f", f$bic),
                                                                  sprintf("%.4f", f$war2)))),
                        check.names = FALSE)
    names(extra) <- names(out)
    out <- rbind(out, extra)
  }
  ft <- flextable(out)
  ft <- align(ft, j = -1, align = "center", part = "all")
  ft <- bold(ft, part = "header")
  ft <- hline(ft, i = length(terms), border = officer::fp_border(width = 0.75))
  ft <- autofit(ft)
  ft
}
fit_of <- function(ks) lapply(ks, function(k) as.list(fit[k, ]))
```

**Purpose.** This note motivates the specification we propose for the growth response to weather shocks. It starts from the symmetric response common in climate econometrics and changes one assumption at a time. All coefficients of every specification are reported in the tables.

# 1. Data and base specification

*Data.* Growth of real GDP per capita from the Penn World Table 11.0 (rgdpna / pop, constant national prices, 2021 PPP US\$). Annual temperature and precipitation from ERA5, aggregated to countries with 2000 population-density weights. The sample has `r format(e$sample[["rows"]], big.mark = ",")` country-years and `r e$sample[["countries"]]` countries over `r e$sample[["first"]]`–`r e$sample[["last"]]`: the rows with all the trailing values below. Recognised non-weather growth outliers are excluded. The `r 100 * src$outliers$share / 2`% lowest and highest growth rates of PWT × ERA5 from `r src$outliers$start_year` (`r format(src$outliers$tails, big.mark = ",")` country-years) are annotated by cause. The `r src$outliers$dropped` not caused by weather are dropped: wars, oil and commodity shocks, reforms and booms, crises, COVID-19 and unidentified causes. `r src$outliers$dropped_sample` of them would otherwise be in the estimation rows. The `r src$outliers$weather_kept` caused by weather (droughts, storms, floods, harvests) stay, as they are the response studied. The agricultural share comes from the **World Bank WDI**: agriculture over the value added of the three sectors, averaged over `r e$horizon[1]`–`r e$horizon[2]` using the previous year's share, so it is constant within a country. PWT does not report it, and a trailing WDI share would drop about 30% of the rows, mostly before 1990.

*Weather deviations.* Each country's weather is measured against its own trailing 20-year climate and scaled by its long-run variability. The trailing mean is used for the deviation; the SD is fixed:

$$x_{v,it} = \frac{v_{it} - \mu^{20}_{v,it}}{\sigma_{v,i}}, \qquad \mu^{20}_{v,it} = \frac{1}{20}\sum_{k=1}^{20} v_{i,t-k}, \qquad v \in \{T, P\}$$

Here $\sigma_{v,i}$ is the SD of $v_{it}$ over `r e$horizon[1]`–`r e$horizon[2]`. The deviation is demeaned by the country's quadratic trend, $d_{v,it} = x_{v,it} - (\hat a_i + \hat b_i t + \hat c_i t^2)$, fitted by OLS for each country. The linear arms split it into positive and negative parts:

$$D^{+}_{v,it} = \max(d_{v,it}, 0), \qquad D^{-}_{v,it} = \max(-d_{v,it}, 0)$$

*Characteristics* (all trailing, apart from the share):

- climate $c_{v,it} = \mu^{20}_{v,it} - \operatorname{med}_j \bar v_j$, the same 20-year trailing mean less the median of the countries' long-run means;
- income $y_{it} = \ln\big(\tfrac{1}{5}\sum_{k=1}^{5} \mathrm{GDPpc}_{i,t-k}\big)$ less its mean over the rows;
- agricultural share $s_i$, less its mean.

*Regression.* Every specification has the form

$$\Delta \ln \mathrm{GDPpc}_{it} = f_T(\cdot) + f_P(\cdot) + \phi_T c_{T,it} + \phi_P c_{P,it} + \phi_y y_{it} + \kappa' C_{it} + \lambda_t + \alpha_i + \delta_i t + \eta_i t^2 + \varepsilon_{it}$$

- $f_T$ and $f_P$ are the weather terms, which change across specifications.
- The levels of trailing climate and income enter every model as controls, so the models differ only in their weather terms.
- $C_{it}$ holds the conflict dummies (minor conflict, war) and the Soviet and Yugoslav collapse years.
- $\lambda_t$ are year effects; $\alpha_i$, $\delta_i t$ and $\eta_i t^2$ are country effects and country linear and quadratic trends.
- Errors are clustered by country.

Coefficients are reported in percentage points of growth per SD of deviation. Interaction coefficients are per unit of the characteristic: °C, m per year, log points of income, or share.

*Comparing models.* Nested models are compared with clustered Wald tests. Non-nested ones are compared by AIC, and a difference is called "indifferent" when a Vuong test clustered by country cannot tell it from noise at 5%.

# 2. Starting point: a symmetric response

The usual specification is linear in the deviation, possibly interacted with the climate:

$$f_v = \beta_v\, d_{v,it} \;\big(+\, \gamma_v\, d_{v,it}\, c_{v,it}\big)$$

This assumes that a hot (wet) year and a cold (dry) year of the same size move growth by the same amount in opposite directions. Nothing in theory or evidence requires that: a dry year and a flood year can both be harmful.

# 3. Test 1: separate hot–cold and wet–dry arms

Each arm gets its own coefficient (and its own climate interaction):

$$f_v = \sum_{a \in \{+,-\}} \big(\beta^{a}_{v} + \gamma^{a}_{v}\, c_{v,it}\big)\, D^{a}_{v,it}$$

The symmetric model is the special case $\beta^{-}_{v} = -\beta^{+}_{v}$ (and $\gamma^{-}_{v} = -\gamma^{+}_{v}$), since $d = D^{+} - D^{-}$. A positive $\beta^{-}$ means that a cold (dry) year *raises* growth.

**Table 1. Symmetric response and arms (pp of growth per SD).**

```{r table1}
coef_table(c("M0: symmetric" = "M0", "M1: arms" = "M1", "M0c: symmetric × climate" = "M0c", "M1c: arms × climate" = "M1c"),
           fits = fit_of(c("M0", "M1", "M0c", "M1c")))
```

*Clustered SEs in brackets; \*\*\* p < 0.01, \*\* p < 0.05, \* p < 0.1.*

**Table 2. Wald tests of symmetry (β⁺ + β⁻ = 0, and γ⁺ + γ⁻ = 0 with the climate interaction).**

```{r table2}
s <- e$tests$symmetry
ft <- flextable(data.frame(Test = rownames(s), F = sprintf("%.2f", s[, "F"]), Restrictions = as.integer(s[, "df"]),
                           `p-value` = pv(s[, "p"]), check.names = FALSE))
autofit(bold(ft, part = "header"))
```

**Result.** Temperature looks symmetric: the warm and cold arms have opposite signs (`r pp(e$coefs$M1$estimate[1])` and +`r pp(e$coefs$M1$estimate[2])` pp), and symmetry is not rejected (p = `r pv(s[1, "p"])`).

Precipitation is not symmetric (p = `r pv(s[2, "p"])`; p = `r pv(s[4, "p"])` with the climate interaction).

- Wet and dry years are *both* harmful: a one-SD wet year changes growth by `r pp(e$coefs$M1$estimate[3])` pp and a one-SD dry year by `r pp(e$coefs$M1$estimate[4])` pp.
- The symmetric term averages them away: `r pp(e$coefs$M0$estimate[2])` pp, p = `r pv(e$coefs$M0$p[2])`.
- With arms, **precipitation is significant at the national level**: joint p = `r pv(e$tests$arms[2, "p"])`, and p = `r pv(e$tests$arms[4, "p"])` with the climate interaction.

By AIC the arms do better (M1 against M0: `r sprintf("%.1f", fit["M1", "aic"] - fit["M0", "aic"])`), although the non-nested Vuong verdict is `r e$verdicts[["M1 vs M0"]]`. Since the models are nested, the symmetry Wald test is the relevant one.

# 4. Test 2: climate or income?

Hot countries are also poorer, so a climate interaction can pick up an income effect. We add income and the agricultural share to the climate interaction:

$$f_v = \sum_{a \in \{+,-\}} \big(\beta^{a}_{v} + \gamma^{a}_{v,c}\, c_{v,it} + \gamma^{a}_{v,y}\, y_{it} + \gamma^{a}_{v,s}\, s_{i}\big)\, D^{a}_{v,it}$$

**Table 3. Climate, income and agricultural-share interactions (pp of growth per SD).**

```{r table3}
coef_table(c("M1c: climate" = "M1c", "M2: climate + income + share" = "M2", "M2b: T climate + income, P climate + share" = "M2b"),
           fits = fit_of(c("M1c", "M2", "M2b")))
```

*Clustered SEs in brackets; \*\*\* p < 0.01, \*\* p < 0.05, \* p < 0.1.*

**Table 4. Joint Wald tests of each characteristic's interactions in M2 (both arms).**

```{r table4}
x <- e$tests$interactions
ft <- flextable(data.frame(Interactions = rownames(x), F = sprintf("%.2f", x[, "F"]), Restrictions = as.integer(x[, "df"]),
                           `p-value` = pv(x[, "p"]), check.names = FALSE))
autofit(bold(ft, part = "header"))
```

**Result.** For temperature, **income** is what matters (p = `r pv(x["T income", "p"])`). Climate (p = `r pv(x["T climate", "p"])`) and share (p = `r pv(x["T share", "p"])`) add little.

For precipitation, the **climate** (p = `r pv(x["P climate", "p"])`) and the **agricultural share** (p = `r pv(x["P share", "p"])`) matter, but income does not (p = `r pv(x["P income", "p"])`). Dry years hurt more where agriculture is a larger share of the economy and less in wetter climates.

Dropping the T × share and P × income terms (M2b) is not rejected: p = `r pv(e$tests$M2b_vs_M2[["p"]])` jointly, with AIC `r sprintf("%+.1f", fit["M2b", "aic"] - fit["M2", "aic"])` and BIC `r sprintf("%+.1f", fit["M2b", "bic"] - fit["M2", "bic"])` against M2. Against M1c (climate only), M2b improves the fit: AIC `r sprintf("%+.1f", fit["M2b", "aic"] - fit["M1c", "aic"])` and BIC `r sprintf("%+.1f", fit["M2b", "bic"] - fit["M1c", "bic"])`.

# 5. A mechanical problem with the linear income interaction

In M2b, the response to a warm year of one SD, at the median climate, is linear in log income:

$$\frac{\partial\, \Delta \ln \mathrm{GDPpc}_{it}}{\partial D^{+}_{T,it}} = \beta^{+}_{T} + \gamma^{+}_{T,y}\, y_{it}$$

- With $\gamma^{+}_{T,y} > 0$, it must change sign at some income and becomes a *gain* for every richer country.
- In M2b this happens at a trailing income of about **US\$`r format(round(e$threshold[["warm"]], -2), big.mark = ",")`** (2021 PPP). That is `r round(100 * e$share_above[["warm"]])`% of the countries in their last sample year.
- For the cold arm the switch is at about US\$`r format(round(e$threshold[["cold"]], -2), big.mark = ",")`.
- The USA would gain `r sprintf("%+.2f", e$responses$warm.estimate[e$responses$iso == "USA" & e$responses$model == "M2b"])` pp of growth from a warm year of one SD (SE `r sprintf("%.2f", e$responses$warm.se[e$responses$iso == "USA" & e$responses$model == "M2b"])`).

The linear form makes this gain inevitable. In projections, where incomes grow, more and more of the world would gain from warming.

```{r fig-income, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = paste0("Response to a warm year of one SD at the median climate, by trailing income: linear income interaction (M2b) against the scaled form with ξ = ", e$xi_preferred, " (Pref). Bands: 95% CI; ticks: the countries' incomes in their last sample year.")}
inc <- exp(seq(log(400), log(150000), length.out = 200))
y <- log(inc) - e$inc_mean
curve_of <- function(k, w) {
  b <- e$coefs[[k]]
  V <- e$vcov[[k]]
  est <- drop(w %*% b$estimate[match(colnames(w), b$term)])
  se <- sqrt(rowSums((w %*% V[colnames(w), colnames(w)]) * w))
  data.frame(income = inc, estimate = 100 * est, low = 100 * (est - 1.96 * se), high = 100 * (est + 1.96 * se))
}
w2 <- cbind(pTM = 1, `pTM:y` = y)
wp <- cbind(`pTM:r` = exp(-(1 - e$xi_preferred) * y))
d <- rbind(cbind(model = "M2b: linear income interaction", curve_of("M2b", w2)),
           cbind(model = paste0("Pref: scaled, ξ = ", e$xi_preferred), curve_of("Pref", wp)))
ggplot(d, aes(income, estimate, colour = model, fill = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), alpha = 0.15, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_rug(data = data.frame(income = exp(e$last$inc_trailing)), aes(x = income), inherit.aes = FALSE,
           sides = "b", alpha = 0.4, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1), breaks = c(500, 2000, 10000, 50000)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#eb6834", "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#eb6834", "#2a78d6"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = "Trailing GDP per capita (2021 PPP US$, log scale)", y = "pp of growth per SD") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) + theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

# 6. Test 3: income as a scaling of the temperature response

Instead of adding income linearly, we let it *scale* the whole temperature response:

$$f_T = \left(\frac{\bar Y}{Y_{it}}\right)^{1-\xi} \sum_{a \in \{+,-\}} \big(\tilde\beta^{a}_{T} + \tilde\gamma^{a}_{T}\, c_{T,it}\big)\, D^{a}_{T,it}$$

$Y_{it}$ is the country's trailing income, and $\bar Y$ = US\$`r format(round(ybar, -1), big.mark = ",")` is a constant: the geometric mean of the trailing income over the rows. A growth effect $\tilde\beta$ at $\bar Y$ is then a loss of $\tilde\beta\, \bar Y^{1-\xi} Y_{it}^{\xi}$ dollars per person, proportional to $Y_{it}^{\xi}$. So $\xi$ is the income elasticity of the dollar loss:

- $\xi = 1$: equal growth effects (the same % at every income; the standard form without income);
- $\xi = 0$: equal losses per capita (the same dollars at every income);
- in between, poorer countries lose a larger % but fewer dollars.

The response cannot change sign with income, so the mechanical problem of Section 5 disappears. Precipitation keeps its climate and share interactions, unscaled.

**Table 5. Income elasticity ξ of the temperature terms, ξ from 0 (equal per-capita dollars) to 1 (equal growth).**

```{r table5}
ft <- flextable(data.frame(
  `ξ` = sprintf("%.1f", g$xi), AIC = sprintf("%.1f", g$aic), `ΔAIC vs best` = sprintf("%+.1f", g$aic - min(g$aic)),
  BIC = sprintf("%.1f", g$bic), `Within adj. R²` = sprintf("%.4f", g$war2),
  `Score test of ξ, p-value` = pv(g$p_score), `Against the best ξ` = g$verdict_vs_best,
  `Against M2b` = g$verdict_vs_M2b, check.names = FALSE))
ft <- bold(ft, i = which(abs(g$xi - e$xi_preferred) < 1e-9), part = "body")
autofit(bold(ft, part = "header"))
```

*Score test: a clustered C(α) test of the given ξ (the derivative of the temperature terms in ξ added to the model). Verdicts: AIC difference beyond noise by the Vuong test clustered by country (5%). The preferred ξ is in bold.*

**Result.** Neither end of the range can be rejected:

- **ξ = 0** has p = `r pv(xi_p(0))` and **ξ = 1** has p = `r pv(xi_p(1))`.
- No ξ fits worse than the best beyond noise, and none differs from M2b.

The data lean towards stronger scaling. AIC is lowest at ξ = 0 (`r sprintf("%+.1f", aic_of(1) - aic_of(0))` from ξ = 0 to ξ = 1), and its unconstrained minimum is at ξ = `r sprintf("%.2f", e$xi_hat)`. The score test also rejects some intermediate values (p < 0.05 for ξ between 0.2 and 0.5). It is a local test of the slope of the fit, and here the fit is not quadratic in ξ, so we read it as weak evidence on where ξ lies. The data do not pin ξ down.

**Estimating ξ directly.** Instead of a grid, ξ can be estimated jointly with the other coefficients by nonlinear least squares. Equal dollars (ξ = 0) and equal growth (ξ = 1) are then restrictions within one model. Given ξ, the model is linear in everything else (fixed effects and trends included), so the estimate minimises over ξ the residual sum of squares of the usual regression (the *profile*):

$$\hat\xi = \arg\min_{\xi} \Big\{ \min_{\tilde\beta,\tilde\gamma,\beta_P,\gamma_P,\phi,\kappa,\lambda,\alpha,\delta,\eta} \textstyle\sum_{it} \hat\varepsilon_{it}(\xi)^2 \Big\}$$

ξ is not restricted to [0, 1]; the search covers −4 to 4. ξ refers to the 5-year trailing income, the income that enters the scaling. The SEs of the conditional regression at $\hat\xi$ treat ξ as known, so inference uses three alternatives:

- **Wald:** the clustered covariance of the full nonlinear model (the Gauss–Newton regression at $\hat\xi$);
- **test inversion:** the ξ not rejected at 5% by a clustered test. The robust test adds every scaled T term times $y_{it}$ to the model at the given ξ and tests these four terms jointly. Under the null they are zero whatever the size of the T response, so the test keeps its size where the response is small. The score test of Table 5 only tests the slope of the profile, so it also accepts at its maxima;
- **country bootstrap:** `r e$xi_nls$boot[["reps"]]` resamples of whole countries, with ξ re-estimated in each.

```{r xi-nls-numbers, include = FALSE}
# The table, the figure and their pieces (xn, G, prof, at, wald_p, draws,
# boot_p, fmt_set, at_low).
source("handout_xi_figure.R")
list2env(xi_helpers(e), environment())
```

**Table 5b. Nonlinear least-squares estimate of ξ: $\hat\xi$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", xn$estimate)` (Wald SE `r sprintf("%.2f", xn$wald[["se"]])`, bootstrap SE `r sprintf("%.2f", xn$boot[["se"]])`). 95% confidence sets and p-values of three values of ξ.**

```{r table5b}
autofit(bold(flextable(xi_table(e, pv)), part = "header"))
```

*Search over ξ in [−4, 4]: a set reaching ±4 continues to the end of the search. Bootstrap: `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * xn$boot[["at_bound"]])`% of the draws end at a bound (`r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * at_low)`% at −4); p-values from the share of draws on either side of the value. Clustered tests: t (Wald, score) or F (robust) with G − 1 = `r G - 1` degrees of freedom.*

```{r fig-xi, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5.4, fig.cap = "Nonlinear least-squares estimate of ξ. Top: profile of the fit (AIC less its minimum; same rows and terms at every ξ). Middle: p-value of the test of each ξ (dotted: 5%). Bottom: country-bootstrap estimates. Shaded: the 95% confidence set of each panel (top: Wald; middle: robust test inverted; bottom: bootstrap percentiles), cut at the bounds of the search. Dashed line: the estimate; grey lines: ξ = 0, 0.6 and 1."}
xi_figure(e)
```

**Result.**

- The estimate is **$\hat\xi$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", xn$estimate)`**: the dollar loss per person falls slightly with income, so poorer countries lose more dollars per person, not only a larger share of income. The profile has a clear global minimum; values of ξ above 1 fit worse by `r sprintf("%.0f", min(prof$aic[prof$xi >= 1]) - min(prof$aic))` AIC points or more.
- **ξ = 0 (equal dollars) is not rejected** by any of the methods (p = `r pv(wald_p(0))` Wald, `r pv(at(0, "p_ar"))` robust, `r pv(boot_p(0))` bootstrap).
- **ξ = 1 (equal growth) is rejected** by the Wald test (p `r sub("^([0-9])", "= \\1", pv(wald_p(1)))`). By the robust test (p = `r pv(at(1, "p_ar"))`) and the bootstrap (p = `r pv(boot_p(1))`) it is at the 5% margin.
- **ξ = 0.6**, an intermediate value, has p = `r pv(wald_p(0.6))` (Wald), `r pv(at(0.6, "p_ar"))` (robust) and `r pv(boot_p(0.6))` (bootstrap).
- ξ is **weakly identified**:
  - the bootstrap SE (`r sprintf("%.2f", xn$boot[["se"]])`) is `r sprintf("%.1f", xn$boot[["se"]] / xn$wald[["se"]])` times the Wald SE, and `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * at_low)`% of the draws run to −4;
  - the robust confidence set is not one interval and is open at both ends;
  - for ξ far from 1 the scaled T terms rest on a few of the poorest or richest countries, so no test has power there, even though the fit is much worse.

  The Wald interval relies on a well-identified ξ and is too narrow here. ξ estimates the combined income elasticity of exposure, relative productivity and vulnerability; separating them needs other data.

Section 12 repeats the estimate with World Bank GDP. There $\hat\xi$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", readRDS(file.path("results", "handout_preferred_specification", "WB", "estimates.rds"))$xi_nls$estimate)`, and the difference from PWT is well within the noise. Section 13 explains the tests and the bootstrap.

**Choice: ξ = `r e$xi_preferred`, equal losses in dollars per person.** The strong income interaction of Section 4 points to some scaling, and equal dollars is the value the evidence supports best:

- it has the lowest AIC on the grid of Table 5, and it is the round value closest to the unconstrained estimates with both GDP sources (Section 12);
- no method rejects it, with either GDP source (here p = `r pv(wald_p(0))` Wald, `r pv(at(0, "p_ar"))` robust, `r pv(boot_p(0))` bootstrap);
- equal growth (ξ = 1) is rejected or at the margin with both sources, and the intermediate ξ = 0.6 is rejected with PWT. These tests reject too often (Section 13), so the evidence against ξ = 0.6 and 1 is weaker than the p-values suggest, but it is against them, not against ξ = 0;
- it has a simple reading: a warm year costs the same dollars per person at every income, so its growth effect falls in proportion to 1/Y.

Because ξ is weakly identified, the other values not rejected remain plausible. In the projections, income growth shrinks the temperature response in proportion to 1/Y, faster than with any ξ above 0.

# 7. Preferred specification

$$\begin{aligned}
\Delta \ln \mathrm{GDPpc}_{it} = {} & \frac{\bar Y}{Y_{it}} \sum_{a \in \{+,-\}} \big(\tilde\beta^{a}_{T} + \tilde\gamma^{a}_{T,c}\, c_{T,it}\big)\, D^{a}_{T,it} \\
& + \sum_{a \in \{+,-\}} \big(\beta^{a}_{P} + \gamma^{a}_{P,c}\, c_{P,it} + \gamma^{a}_{P,s}\, s_{i}\big)\, D^{a}_{P,it} \\
& + \phi_T c_{T,it} + \phi_P c_{P,it} + \phi_y y_{it} + \kappa' C_{it} + \lambda_t + \alpha_i + \delta_i t + \eta_i t^2 + \varepsilon_{it}
\end{aligned}$$

The specification combines:

- the temperature arms scaled by income with ξ = `r e$xi_preferred` (equal losses in dollars per person), interacted with the climate;
- the precipitation arms interacted with the climate and the agricultural share;
- climate as the 20-year trailing mean (deviations and interactions), income as the 5-year trailing mean, and the fixed long-run SD.

It fits like M2b (`r e$verdicts[["Pref vs M2b"]]`; AIC `r sprintf("%+.1f", fit["Pref", "aic"] - fit["M2b", "aic"])`, BIC `r sprintf("%+.1f", fit["Pref", "bic"] - fit["M2b", "bic"])`) with two fewer terms.

**Table 6. Preferred specification (ξ = `r e$xi_preferred`), two other values of ξ, and M2b (pp of growth per SD).**

```{r table6}
cf <- c(e$coefs, list(xi06 = e$coefs_scaled[["xi=0.6"]], xi1 = e$coefs_scaled[["xi=1.0"]]))
f <- function(k) {
  if (k %in% rownames(fit)) return(as.list(fit[k, ]))
  r <- g[abs(g$xi - c(xi06 = 0.6, xi1 = 1)[[k]]) < 1e-9, ]
  list(rows = fit["Pref", "rows"], countries = fit["Pref", "countries"], aic = r$aic, bic = r$bic, war2 = r$war2)
}
coef_table(stats::setNames(c("Pref", "xi06", "xi1", "M2b"),
                           c(paste0("Preferred: ξ = ", e$xi_preferred, " (equal dollars)"), "ξ = 0.6",
                             "ξ = 1 (equal growth)", "M2b: linear income")),
           coefs = cf, fits = lapply(c("Pref", "xi06", "xi1", "M2b"), f))
```

*Clustered SEs in brackets; \*\*\* p < 0.01, \*\* p < 0.05, \* p < 0.1. The scaled coefficients are the responses at income Ȳ.*

**Table 7. Responses to a one-SD year in selected countries (pp of growth; clustered SE in brackets), at their trailing climate and income in the last sample year.**

```{r table7}
r <- e$responses
cell <- function(est, se) sprintf("%+.2f (%.2f)", est, se)
labels <- c(M1c = "M1c: climate", M2b = "M2b: linear income", Pref = "Preferred")
ft <- flextable(data.frame(
  Country = countrycode::countrycode(r$iso, "iso3c", "country.name"),
  `Income (US$)` = format(round(r$income, -1), big.mark = ","), Model = labels[r$model],
  Warm = cell(r$warm.estimate, r$warm.se), Cold = cell(r$cold.estimate, r$cold.se),
  Wet = cell(r$wet.estimate, r$wet.se), Dry = cell(r$dry.estimate, r$dry.se), check.names = FALSE))
ft <- merge_v(ft, j = c("Country", "Income (US$)"))
ft <- hline(ft, i = seq(3, nrow(r) - 1, by = 3), border = officer::fp_border(width = 0.5, color = "grey60"))
ft <- valign(ft, j = 1:2, valign = "top")
autofit(bold(ft, part = "header"))
```

**Reading.** Under the preferred specification a warm year is harmful everywhere. The loss shrinks with income: `r sprintf("%+.2f", r$warm.estimate[r$iso == "BDI" & r$model == "Pref"])` pp in Burundi and `r sprintf("%+.2f", r$warm.estimate[r$iso == "USA" & r$model == "Pref"])` pp in the USA, against `r sprintf("%+.2f", r$warm.estimate[r$iso == "USA" & r$model == "M2b"])` pp with the linear income term. Dry years cost the most where agriculture is large (Burundi `r sprintf("%+.2f", r$dry.estimate[r$iso == "BDI" & r$model == "Pref"])` pp).

The linear share interaction has the same kind of problem on a smaller scale. For economies with little agriculture in wet climates, a dry year has a small positive, not significant, effect (Brazil and the USA, about +0.16 pp).

# 8. Linear or quadratic arms?

The arms enter linearly so far. The quadratic alternative squares them, with the same interactions and the same income scaling:

$$f_T = \frac{\bar Y}{Y_{it}} \sum_{a \in \{+,-\}} \big(\tilde\beta^{a}_{T} + \tilde\gamma^{a}_{T,c}\, c_{T,it}\big) \big(D^{a}_{T,it}\big)^{2}, \qquad f_P = \sum_{a \in \{+,-\}} \big(\beta^{a}_{P} + \gamma^{a}_{P,c}\, c_{P,it} + \gamma^{a}_{P,s}\, s_{i}\big) \big(D^{a}_{P,it}\big)^{2}$$

The two forms are not nested, so we use two tests:

- a Vuong test of the two models (same number of terms);
- Wald tests in the model with both the linear and the squared arms: either set of terms set to zero.

**Table 8. Linear and quadratic arms in the preferred specification (pp of growth per SD, or per SD squared).**

```{r table8}
coef_table(c("Linear arms (preferred)" = "Pref", "Quadratic arms" = "PrefQ"), fits = fit_of(c("Pref", "PrefQ")))
```

*Clustered SEs in brackets; \*\*\* p < 0.01, \*\* p < 0.05, \* p < 0.1.*

**Table 9. Wald tests in the model with both linear and squared arms (`r fit["PrefLQ", "terms"]` terms).**

```{r table9}
q <- e$tests$quadratic
ft <- flextable(data.frame(`Null hypothesis` = rownames(q), F = sprintf("%.2f", q[, "F"]),
                           Restrictions = as.integer(q[, "df"]), `p-value` = pv(q[, "p"]), check.names = FALSE))
autofit(bold(ft, part = "header"))
```

**Result. With ξ = `r e$xi_preferred`, the data lean towards quadratic arms for temperature.**

- In the model with both, dropping the squared terms is rejected (p = `r pv(q[1, "p"])`; for T alone p = `r pv(q[2, "p"])`), and dropping the linear terms is not (p = `r pv(q[4, "p"])`). For P neither set is needed given the other (p = `r pv(q[3, "p"])` and `r pv(q[6, "p"])`).
- The quadratic form has the lower AIC (`r sprintf("%+.1f", fit["PrefQ", "aic"] - fit["Pref", "aic"])`) and BIC, but the Vuong test of the two is `r e$verdicts[["PrefQ vs Pref"]]`.
- With ξ = 0.6 neither form could be rejected (p = 0.39 and 0.94).

**The quadratic specification is therefore at least as well supported as the linear one**, and it changes how much the *rate* of warming matters relative to its *level*:

- The deviations are measured from the trailing 20-year climate, so gradual warming shows up mostly as a moving climate. That is a level, acting through the climate interactions.
- Only the part of warming faster than the trailing mean can follow shows up as a deviation. That is the rate.
- With linear arms, the same total warming costs about the same however fast it arrives.
- With quadratic arms, small deviations (slow warming) cost less and large deviations (fast warming) cost more than in the linear model.

Table 10 shows this at the country level. The quadratic responses are similar or smaller at one SD, but they grow fourfold from one to two SD, against twofold for linear arms. At two SD the quadratic response is larger for warm and dry years (Burundi: warm `r sprintf("%+.2f", e$responses_q$warm.estimate[e$responses_q$iso == "BDI" & e$responses_q$size == 2 & e$responses_q$model == "PrefQ"])` against `r sprintf("%+.2f", e$responses_q$warm.estimate[e$responses_q$iso == "BDI" & e$responses_q$size == 2 & e$responses_q$model == "Pref"])` pp).

**Table 10. Responses to a one- and a two-SD year, linear and quadratic arms (pp of growth; clustered SE in brackets).**

```{r table10}
rq <- e$responses_q[e$responses_q$iso %in% c("BDI", "IND", "BRA", "USA"), ]
cell <- function(est, se) sprintf("%+.2f (%.2f)", est, se)
ft <- flextable(data.frame(
  Country = countrycode::countrycode(rq$iso, "iso3c", "country.name"), `Size (SD)` = rq$size,
  Arms = ifelse(rq$model == "Pref", "linear", "quadratic"),
  Warm = cell(rq$warm.estimate, rq$warm.se), Cold = cell(rq$cold.estimate, rq$cold.se),
  Wet = cell(rq$wet.estimate, rq$wet.se), Dry = cell(rq$dry.estimate, rq$dry.se), check.names = FALSE))
ft <- merge_v(ft, j = c("Country", "Size (SD)"))
ft <- valign(ft, j = 1:2, valign = "top")
autofit(bold(ft, part = "header"))
```

# 9. Global GDP projections: fixed or evolving income and agricultural share

We project the linear preferred specification under SSP1-2.6 and SSP2-4.5, each with its own SSP. The projections use the response explorer's code.

*Warming.* The global path is the FaIR median (AR6 calibration). It is scaled to each country by its CMIP6 pattern: the median slope for T, and the median relative slope times the country's long-run P for P.

*Climate characteristics.* The deviations are measured against the trailing 20-year mean of the projected anomalies and divided by the country's long-run SD. The climate in the interactions moves with the same trailing mean, so climate evolves in both variants below.

*Income and agricultural share.* Two variants:

- **fixed**: held at the country's 2025 values;
- **SSP**: they follow the SSP, as trailing means of the country's history continued with the SSP's relative change (5 years for income, 20 for the share).

*Losses.* They accumulate from 2025 against a world without further climate change. The global loss weights the countries by the SSP's GDP of each year. It covers `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * pr$coverage[[1]])`% of the SSP's world GDP (`r pr$n[[1]]` countries). The 95% CI comes from the clustered covariance of the coefficients.

```{r fig-global, fig.width = 6.8, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Global GDP loss against no climate change, linear preferred specification. Left: income and agricultural share fixed at their 2025 values; right: following the SSP. The climate evolves in both. Bands: 95% CI of the coefficients."}
gl <- pr$global
gl$econ <- factor(gl$econ, levels = unname(pr$econ_labels))
ggplot(gl, aes(year, estimate, colour = scenario, fill = scenario)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), alpha = 0.12, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~econ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("SSP1-2.6" = "#5598e7", "SSP2-4.5" = "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("SSP1-2.6" = "#5598e7", "SSP2-4.5" = "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "World GDP against no climate change (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) + theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

**Table 11. Global GDP loss (% against no climate change; 95% CI), linear preferred specification.**

```{r table11}
x <- pr$global[pr$global$year %in% c(2050, 2100), ]
cell <- function(r) sprintf("%+.2f [%+.2f, %+.2f]", r$estimate, r$low, r$high)
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(x, list(x$scenario, x$econ), drop = TRUE), function(r) {
  data.frame(Scenario = r$scenario[1], `Income and share` = sub("Income and share ", "", r$econ[1]),
             `2050` = cell(r[r$year == 2050, ]), `2100` = cell(r[r$year == 2100, ]), check.names = FALSE)
}))
tab <- tab[order(tab$Scenario), ]
autofit(bold(flextable(tab), part = "header"))
```

```{r numbers-proj, include = FALSE}
g100 <- function(s, k) pr$global$estimate[pr$global$scenario == s & pr$global$year == 2100 & pr$global$econ == pr$econ_labels[[k]]]
```

**Result.** Letting income and the share evolve reduces the global loss in 2100 from `r sprintf("%.1f", g100("SSP2-4.5", "fixed"))`% to `r sprintf("%.1f", g100("SSP2-4.5", "SSP"))`% under SSP2-4.5, and from `r sprintf("%.1f", g100("SSP1-2.6", "fixed"))`% to `r sprintf("%.1f", g100("SSP1-2.6", "SSP"))`% under SSP1-2.6. Two things drive this:

- as countries grow richer, the temperature response shrinks with the income scaling ($\xi$ = `r e$xi_preferred`: in proportion to 1/Y);
- as their agricultural share falls, the dry-year response shrinks.

```{r numbers-proj-old, include = FALSE}
pr_old <- readRDS(file.path("results", "handout_preferred_specification", "projections_xi06.rds"))
g100_old <- function(s, k) pr_old$global$estimate[pr_old$global$scenario == s & pr_old$global$year == 2100 & pr_old$global$econ == pr_old$econ_labels[[k]]]
c45 <- pr$countries_2100[pr$countries_2100$scenario == "SSP2-4.5" & pr$countries_2100$econ == pr$econ_labels[["fixed"]], ]
c45 <- c45[order(c45$loss_T), ]
```

With ξ = 0.6, the previous choice, the losses were larger and less precise: `r sprintf("%.1f", g100_old("SSP2-4.5", "fixed"))`% (fixed) and `r sprintf("%.1f", g100_old("SSP2-4.5", "SSP"))`% (SSP) under SSP2-4.5 in 2100. Equal dollars concentrates the losses on the poorest countries. With income and share fixed under SSP2-4.5, temperature alone costs `r paste(sprintf("%s %.0f%%", countrycode::countrycode(c45$iso3[1:4], "iso3c", "country.name", custom_match = c(COD = "DR Congo")), c45$loss_T[1:4]), collapse = ", ")` by 2100, and less than `r sprintf("%.1f", ceiling(10 * max(abs(c45$loss_T[c45$iso3 %in% c("USA", "DEU", "FRA", "GBR", "JPN", "NOR", "CHE")]))) / 10)`% in the richest economies.

Most of the damage comes from temperature. Precipitation matters mainly in the drier agricultural economies of the Sahel and West Africa (Guinea-Bissau, Gambia, Niger, Chad), and in India. In very wet climates with little agriculture it adds a small gain (Costa Rica, Colombia, Panama).

```{r maps, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.1, fig.cap = c("GDP loss in 2100 against no climate change under SSP2-4.5, by country: impact of the temperature deviations, of the precipitation deviations, and total. Top: income and share fixed at 2025; bottom: following the SSP. Each component has its own colour scale (in %, the same for the two rows), capped at the 98th percentile of its absolute losses.", "As the previous figure, under SSP1-2.6.")}
world <- SCEN_world <- readRDS(file.path("results", "response_explorer", "scenarios.rds"))$world
world <- world[world$iso3 != "ATA", ]
# `countries`: the 2100 losses to map; the colour scales come from those
# without variability, so the maps with it are comparable.
map_of <- function(scen, countries = pr$countries_2100) {
  scale_ref <- pr$countries_2100[pr$countries_2100$scenario == scen, ]
  c2 <- countries[countries$scenario == scen, ]
  long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(loss_T = "Temperature", loss_P = "Precipitation", loss = "Total"), function(k) {
    data.frame(iso3 = c2$iso3, econ = c2$econ, component = k, value = c2[[names(which(c(loss_T = "Temperature",
      loss_P = "Precipitation", loss = "Total") == k))]])
  }))
  long$component <- factor(long$component, levels = c("Temperature", "Precipitation", "Total"))
  long$econ <- factor(sub("Income and share ", "", long$econ), levels = c("fixed at 2025", "follow the SSP"))
  grid <- expand.grid(econ = levels(long$econ), component = levels(long$component), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  sfl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
    w <- world
    v <- long[long$econ == grid$econ[i] & long$component == grid$component[i], ]
    w$value <- v$value[match(w$iso3, v$iso3)]
    w$econ <- grid$econ[i]
    w$component <- grid$component[i]
    w
  }))
  sfl$econ <- factor(sfl$econ, levels = levels(long$econ))
  sfl$component <- factor(sfl$component, levels = levels(long$component))
  # One colour scale per component (the same for the two rows), capped at the
  # 98th percentile of its absolute losses.
  panels <- lapply(levels(long$component), function(k) {
    x <- sfl[sfl$component == k, ]
    column <- c(Temperature = "loss_T", Precipitation = "loss_P", Total = "loss")[[k]]
    limit <- stats::quantile(abs(scale_ref[[column]]), 0.98, na.rm = TRUE)
    ggplot(x) +
      geom_sf(aes(fill = value), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.05) +
      facet_grid(econ ~ component, switch = "y") +
      coord_sf(expand = FALSE, ylim = c(-6.2e6, 8.4e6)) +
      scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#e34948", mid = "#f0efec", high = "#2a78d6", midpoint = 0,
                           limits = c(-limit, limit), oob = scales::squish, na.value = "#d9d8d4",
                           name = "%", breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(4)) +
      theme_void(base_size = 8) +
      theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.width = grid::unit(0.9, "cm"),
            legend.key.height = grid::unit(0.25, "cm"), strip.text = element_text(size = 8),
            strip.text.y.left = if (k == "Temperature") element_text(angle = 90, size = 8) else element_blank())
  })
  patchwork::wrap_plots(panels, nrow = 1)
}
print(map_of("SSP2-4.5"))
print(map_of("SSP1-2.6"))
```

# 10. Termination of geoengineering under SSP2-4.5: quadratic specification

Perfect geoengineering holds global warming at `r pr$held` °C from 2025, as the response explorer's termination paths do. After termination in 2050 or 2070, the temperature catches up with the SSP2-4.5 path with a characteristic time of `r pr$tau` years:

$$G(t) = B(t) - \max\big(B(T) - H, 0\big)\, e^{-(t - T)/\tau}$$

Here $B$ is the SSP2-4.5 path, $H$ the held level and $T$ the termination year. We use the quadratic specification, since that is where the rate of warming matters, with income and share fixed at 2025 or following SSP2. The linear specification is reported for comparison.

```{r fig-gmt, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 2.4, fig.cap = "Global warming above 1850–1900 under SSP2-4.5 (FaIR median), with geoengineering sustained at 1.5 °C and terminated in 2050 or 2070."}
cols <- c("No geoengineering (SSP2-4.5)" = "#52514e", "Geoengineering sustained at 1.5 C" = "#2a78d6",
          "Terminated in 2050" = "#f0a35e", "Terminated in 2070" = "#c4511a")
gp <- pr$gmt_paths[pr$gmt_paths$year >= 2000, ]
gp$path <- factor(gp$path, levels = names(cols))
ggplot(gp, aes(year, warming, colour = path)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Warming (°C)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) + theme(legend.position = "right", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

```{r fig-termination, fig.width = 6.8, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Global GDP loss against no climate change under SSP2-4.5 with termination of geoengineering, quadratic specification. Left: income and agricultural share fixed at 2025; right: following SSP2. Bands: 95% CI of the coefficients."}
tq <- pr$termination[pr$termination$model == "Quadratic arms", ]
tq$path <- factor(tq$path, levels = names(cols))
tq$econ <- factor(tq$econ, levels = unname(pr$econ_labels))
ggplot(tq, aes(year, estimate, colour = path, fill = path)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), alpha = 0.08, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~econ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols, name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols, name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "World GDP against no climate change (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
  theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank()) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2), fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2))
```

**Table 12. Global GDP loss with termination of geoengineering under SSP2-4.5 (% against no climate change; 95% CI).**

```{r table12}

cell <- function(r) sprintf("%+.2f [%+.2f, %+.2f]", r$estimate, r$low, r$high)
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(tt, list(tt$model, tt$econ, tt$path), drop = TRUE), function(r) {
  data.frame(Arms = sub(" arms", "", r$model[1]), `Income and share` = sub("Income and share ", "", r$econ[1]),
             Path = r$path[1], `2050` = cell(r[r$year == 2050, ]), `2070` = cell(r[r$year == 2070, ]),
             `2100` = cell(r[r$year == 2100, ]), check.names = FALSE)
}))
tab <- tab[order(tab$Arms != "Quadratic", tab$`Income and share`, match(tab$Path, names(cols))), ]
ft <- merge_v(flextable(tab), j = c("Arms", "Income and share"))

autofit(bold(ft, part = "header"))

```{r numbers-term, include = FALSE}
tv <- function(model, econ, path, year) {
  x <- pr$termination
  x$estimate[x$model == model & x$econ == pr$econ_labels[[econ]] & x$path == path & x$year == year]
}
```

**Result.** With quadratic arms, termination is costly because of how fast the catch-up is.

- **Terminated in 2050**, with income and share fixed: the loss reaches `r sprintf("%.1f", tv("Quadratic arms", "fixed", "Terminated in 2050", 2070))`% by 2070. Without geoengineering it would be `r sprintf("%.1f", tv("Quadratic arms", "fixed", "No geoengineering (SSP2-4.5)", 2070))`%, and with sustained geoengineering `r sprintf("%.1f", tv("Quadratic arms", "fixed", "Geoengineering sustained at 1.5 C", 2070))`%.
- **By 2100** the loss is `r sprintf("%.1f", tv("Quadratic arms", "fixed", "Terminated in 2050", 2100))`% after termination in 2050 and `r sprintf("%.1f", tv("Quadratic arms", "fixed", "Terminated in 2070", 2100))`% after termination in 2070. Both are above the `r sprintf("%.1f", tv("Quadratic arms", "fixed", "No geoengineering (SSP2-4.5)", 2100))`% of gradual warming to the same temperature. The later the termination, the larger the jump and the cost.
- **With income and share following SSP2**, all losses are much smaller and termination adds little: `r sprintf("%.1f", tv("Quadratic arms", "SSP", "Terminated in 2070", 2100))`% in 2100 after termination in 2070, against `r sprintf("%.1f", tv("Quadratic arms", "SSP", "No geoengineering (SSP2-4.5)", 2100))`% without geoengineering. With equal-dollar scaling, incomes have grown enough by the catch-up to shrink the response.
- **With linear arms**, termination costs about the same as never deploying: `r sprintf("%.1f", tv("Linear arms", "fixed", "Terminated in 2070", 2100))`% against `r sprintf("%.1f", tv("Linear arms", "fixed", "No geoengineering (SSP2-4.5)", 2100))`% in 2100, with income and share fixed. Only the level of warming matters in the long run.

The choice between the two forms, which the data cannot make, decides whether termination shocks matter, as long as the climate is the forced signal alone. Section 11 adds natural variability.

# 11. Natural variability

So far each country's climate in the projections is the forced signal alone: a smooth path with no year-to-year variability. The real climate varies around that path. The noise averages to zero, but the response is not linear in the anomaly, so it changes the expected loss:

- the kink between the warm and cold (wet and dry) arms;
- the squared arms;
- the trailing climate in the interactions, which moves with the noise.

*Noise.* For each country and $v \in \{T, P\}$, the noise pool is the annual series less the country's own quadratic trend over `r e$horizon[1]`–`r e$horizon[2]`:

$$\nu_{v,i\tau} = v_{i\tau} - (\hat a_{v,i} + \hat b_{v,i} \tau + \hat c_{v,i} \tau^2), \qquad \tau = `r e$horizon[1]`, \dots, `r e$horizon[2]`$$

A noise path draws a historical year $\tau_k$ for each projection year $k$. The anomaly is the forced signal $S_{v,ik}$ plus the noise of that year, from 1994 so that the trailing means of 2025 already contain noise. The counterfactual has the noise alone. The loss is the difference:

$$L_i(t) = \exp\Big(\sum_{k=2025}^{t} \big[\, g_i\big(S_{ik} + \nu_{i\tau_k}\big) - g_i\big(\nu_{i\tau_k}\big) \big]\Big) - 1$$

Here $g_i$ is the growth effect of the specification, including the trailing mean, the deviation and the interactions. The same noise path enters both terms, so the noise affects the loss only through the non-linearity of $g_i$.

The years can be drawn in three ways:

- **independently** for each country;
- **jointly**: the same calendar year for every country. This keeps the spatial correlation of the weather, which is local for P and both local and global for T;
- **jointly in 5-year blocks** of consecutive years, which also keeps their persistence.

We use `r format(pr$n_paths, big.mark = ",")` noise paths. Each path is paired with a draw of the coefficients, so the 95% CI includes both sources of uncertainty. The estimate is the mean over the paths at the estimated coefficients. The variability range is the 2.5–97.5% range of the paths alone, at the estimated coefficients. `r pr$n_noise` countries have the complete historical climate.

**Table 13. Global GDP loss under SSP2-4.5 with income and share fixed at 2025, by way of drawing the noise (% against no climate change; 95% CI, then the range over the noise paths). T and P: the losses of each variable alone in 2100.**

```{r table13}
nv <- pr$noise_versions
nv$noise <- factor(nv$noise, levels = c("none", "iid", "joint", "blocks"),
                   labels = c("None (forced signal)", "Independent years", "Joint years", "Joint 5-year blocks"))
cell <- function(r) {
  out <- sprintf("%+.2f [%+.2f, %+.2f]", r$estimate, r$low, r$high)
  ifelse(is.na(r$noise_low), out, paste0(out, "\n(", sprintf("%+.2f, %+.2f", r$noise_low, r$noise_high), ")"))
}
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(nv, list(nv$model, nv$noise), drop = TRUE), function(r) {
  r100 <- r[r$year == 2100, ]
  data.frame(Arms = sub(" arms", "", r$model[1]), Noise = as.character(r$noise[1]), noise_order = as.integer(r$noise[1]),
             `2050` = cell(r[r$year == 2050, ]), `2100` = cell(r100),
             `T, 2100` = sprintf("%+.2f", r100$T), `P, 2100` = sprintf("%+.2f", r100$P), check.names = FALSE)
}))
tab <- tab[order(tab$Arms, tab$noise_order), names(tab) != "noise_order"]
ft <- merge_v(flextable(tab), j = "Arms")
ft <- valign(ft, j = 1, valign = "top")
autofit(bold(ft, part = "header"))
```

```{r numbers-noise, include = FALSE}
nvv <- function(model, noise, year, column = "estimate") {
  nv0 <- pr$noise_versions
  nv0[[column]][nv0$model == model & nv0$noise == noise & nv0$year == year]
}
cf <- function(k, term) 100 * e$coefs[[k]]$estimate[e$coefs[[k]]$term == term]
```

**Result. Variability changes the loss, but how it is drawn does not.**

- **The way of drawing barely matters.** Spatial correlation and persistence leave the mean loss unchanged (each country still draws from its own distribution). Joint draws widen the range over the noise paths, but only slightly: the same noise is in the warming run and in the counterfactual, so even a run of globally hot years mostly cancels out. Coefficient uncertainty dominates the CI.
- **With linear arms the loss is smaller**: `r sprintf("%.1f", nvv("Linear arms", "blocks", 2100))`% in 2100 against `r sprintf("%.1f", nvv("Linear arms", "none", 2100))`% without noise. Without noise, warming is a positive deviation and hits only the warm arm (`r sprintf("%+.2f", cf("Pref", "pTM:r"))` pp per SD). With noise, a small shift of the climate moves deviations on both sides of zero, so its effect is a probability-weighted mix of the warm arm and the cold arm. The cold arm is small and not significant (`r sprintf("%+.2f", cf("Pref", "nTM:r"))` pp per SD of cold). A year shifted out of it changes growth by minus that amount, so near zero the slope is about the average of `r sprintf("%+.2f", cf("Pref", "pTM:r"))` and `r sprintf("%+.2f", -cf("Pref", "nTM:r"))`, much less steep than the warm arm alone. Precipitation turns from a loss to a small gain (`r sprintf("%+.2f", nvv("Linear arms", "blocks", 2100, "P"))`%). Without noise a wetter climate only adds wet years. With noise it also removes dry years, which hurt more (`r sprintf("%+.2f", cf("Pref", "nRR"))` against `r sprintf("%+.2f", cf("Pref", "pRR"))` pp per SD).
- **With quadratic arms the loss is larger**: `r sprintf("%.1f", nvv("Quadratic arms", "blocks", 2100))`% against `r sprintf("%.1f", nvv("Quadratic arms", "none", 2100))`%. Without noise a slow shift $s$ costs only $s^2$, almost nothing. With noise, $E[(x+s)_+^2] - E[x_+^2] \approx 2s\,E[x_+]$: the shift costs in proportion to its size, as in a linear model.
- **The two forms now give similar losses** (`r sprintf("%.1f", nvv("Linear arms", "blocks", 2100))`% and `r sprintf("%.1f", nvv("Quadratic arms", "blocks", 2100))`% in 2100, against `r sprintf("%.1f", nvv("Linear arms", "none", 2100))`% and `r sprintf("%.1f", nvv("Quadratic arms", "none", 2100))`% without noise). Natural variability smooths both responses around zero, so the choice of form, which the data cannot make, matters much less once the climate is realistic.

We use joint 5-year blocks below, the most realistic of the three.

```{r fig-global-noise, fig.width = 6.8, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Global GDP loss against no climate change, linear preferred specification, with natural variability (joint 5-year blocks; solid) and without it (dashed, as in Section 9). Left: income and agricultural share fixed at 2025; right: following the SSP. Bands: 95% of the coefficient draws, each with its noise path."}
gn <- rbind(cbind(pr$global_noise[, c("scenario", "econ", "year", "estimate", "low", "high")], climate = "with variability"),
            cbind(pr$global[, c("scenario", "econ", "year", "estimate", "low", "high")], climate = "forced signal only"))
gn$econ <- factor(gn$econ, levels = unname(pr$econ_labels))
gn$climate <- factor(gn$climate, levels = c("with variability", "forced signal only"))
ggplot(gn, aes(year, estimate, colour = scenario, fill = scenario, linetype = climate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_ribbon(data = gn[gn$climate == "with variability", ], aes(ymin = low, ymax = high), alpha = 0.12, colour = NA) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~econ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("SSP1-2.6" = "#5598e7", "SSP2-4.5" = "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("SSP1-2.6" = "#5598e7", "SSP2-4.5" = "#eb6834"), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("with variability" = "solid", "forced signal only" = "22"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "World GDP against no climate change (%)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 9) + theme(legend.position = "top", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

```{r numbers-term-noise, include = FALSE}

  x$estimate[x$model == model & x$econ == pr$econ_labels[[econ]] & x$path == path & x$year == year]
}

```{r table15}
tt <- pr$termination_noise[pr$termination_noise$year %in% c(2050, 2070, 2100), ]
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(tt, list(tt$model, tt$econ, tt$path), drop = TRUE), function(r) {

             `2100` = cell(r[r$year == 2100, ]), check.names = FALSE)
}))
