```{r numbers-term-gap, include = FALSE}
# Extra loss in 2100 of termination in `year` over no geoengineering (pp).
gap <- function(model, econ, year, noise = TRUE) {
  f <- if (noise) tvn else tv
  f(model, econ, paste("Terminated in", year), 2100) - f(model, econ, "No geoengineering (SSP2-4.5)", 2100)
}
```

**Result. With variability, termination costs more than never deploying under both forms, and the gap between the forms narrows.**

- **Quadratic arms, income and share fixed:** termination in 2070 costs `r sprintf("%.1f", tvn("Quadratic arms", "fixed", "Terminated in 2070", 2100))`% by 2100, against `r sprintf("%.1f", tvn("Quadratic arms", "fixed", "No geoengineering (SSP2-4.5)", 2100))`% without geoengineering. That is `r sprintf("%.1f", -gap("Quadratic arms", "fixed", 2070))` pp more, against `r sprintf("%.1f", -gap("Quadratic arms", "fixed", 2070, FALSE))` pp without variability. Termination in 2050 costs `r sprintf("%.1f", -gap("Quadratic arms", "fixed", 2050))` pp more (`r sprintf("%.1f", -gap("Quadratic arms", "fixed", 2050, FALSE))` pp without variability). The extra cost of a late termination survives, but it is smaller, because the gradual path is now also costly.
- **Linear arms, income and share fixed:** termination in 2070 now costs `r sprintf("%.1f", -gap("Linear arms", "fixed", 2070))` pp more than never deploying (`r sprintf("%.1f", tvn("Linear arms", "fixed", "Terminated in 2070", 2100))`% against `r sprintf("%.1f", tvn("Linear arms", "fixed", "No geoengineering (SSP2-4.5)", 2100))`%). Without variability the two were the same. With noise, the expected linear-arm response is convex in the shift: a shift within the noise has about the average slope of the two arms, and a shift beyond it the full warm-arm slope. A fast catch-up therefore costs more than gradual warming, so the rate of warming matters with linear arms too.
- **With income and share following SSP2**, termination in 2070 makes no difference by 2100 with either form (`r sprintf("%+.1f", gap("Quadratic arms", "SSP", 2070))` pp of GDP against never deploying with quadratic arms, `r sprintf("%+.1f", gap("Linear arms", "SSP", 2070))` pp with linear arms): growing incomes shrink the response before the catch-up arrives.
- **Sustained geoengineering:** the loss by 2100 is `r sprintf("%.1f", tvn("Quadratic arms", "fixed", "Geoengineering sustained at 1.5 C", 2100))`% (quadratic) and `r sprintf("%.1f", tvn("Linear arms", "fixed", "Geoengineering sustained at 1.5 C", 2100))`% (linear), against `r sprintf("%.1f", tv("Quadratic arms", "fixed", "Geoengineering sustained at 1.5 C", 2100))`% and `r sprintf("%.1f", tv("Linear arms", "fixed", "Geoengineering sustained at 1.5 C", 2100))`% without variability.

The conclusion of Section 10 holds in a weaker form. With realistic variability, termination shocks matter under both forms. How much they matter still depends on the form, by a factor of about `r sprintf("%.0f", gap("Quadratic arms", "fixed", 2070) / gap("Linear arms", "fixed", 2070))` for termination in 2070 with income and share fixed.

# 12. Robustness of ξ: World Bank GDP

```{r wb-setup, include = FALSE}
base_dir <- file.path("results", "handout_preferred_specification")
wbe <- readRDS(file.path(base_dir, "WB", "estimates.rds"))
pce <- readRDS(file.path(base_dir, "PWT_common", "estimates.rds"))
wce <- readRDS(file.path(base_dir, "WB_common", "estimates.rds"))
gr <- src$growth
lv <- src$levels
dx <- wce$xi_nls$boot_draws - pce$xi_nls$boot_draws
sw <- pce$xi_nls$swaps
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
name_of <- function(iso) countrycode::countrycode(iso, "iso3c", "country.name")
```

The estimate of ξ is repeated with World Bank GDP per capita (WDI NY.GDP.PCAP.KD, constant 2015 US\$). Everything else is unchanged: ERA5 weather, the same outliers (the PWT tails of Section 1), the same specification, the same search over ξ and the same bootstrap.

**How the two sources differ: growth.** Both series are real growth at constant national prices. Their gap therefore does not come from PPP against exchange rates, but from the national-accounts sources, vintages, splices and population series. On the `r format(gr$rows, big.mark = ",")` country-years both cover, the growth rates correlate at `r sprintf("%.2f", gr$cor)`. In most years they agree (median absolute gap `r sprintf("%.2f", gr$median_abs)` pp), but the gap exceeds 2 pp in `r pct(gr$over[["2"]])` of them (SD of the gap `r sprintf("%.1f", gr$sd_gap)` pp, against `r sprintf("%.1f", gr$sd_pwt)` pp for growth itself).

**Table 16. Gap between PWT and World Bank growth (pp), by group: SD, mean absolute gap and share of years with a gap above 2 pp.**

```{r table16}
lab_rows <- function(x, group, label) {
  data.frame(Group = group, ` ` = label, Rows = x$rows, SD = sprintf("%.2f", x$sd), `Mean |gap|` = sprintf("%.2f", x$mean_abs),
             `Gap > 2 pp` = pct(x$over_2pp), check.names = FALSE)
}
co <- gr$conflict_outlier
tab <- rbind(
  lab_rows(gr$decade, "Decade", gr$decade$decade),
  lab_rows(gr$region, "Region", gr$region$region),
  lab_rows(gr$quintile, "WB income quintile", paste0("Q", gr$quintile$quintile, c(" (poorest)", "", "", "", " (richest)"))),
  lab_rows(co, "Year type", paste0(ifelse(co$conflict, "conflict", "no conflict"), ", ",
                                   ifelse(co$outlier_5, "dropped outlier", "kept"))))
ft <- merge_v(flextable(tab), j = "Group")
ft <- valign(ft, j = 1, valign = "top")
autofit(bold(ft, part = "header"))
```

- **Mostly noise.** Country effects explain `r pct(gr$r2[["country"]])` of the gap and year effects `r pct(gr$r2[["year"]])`. Its first-order autocorrelation is `r sprintf("%.2f", gr$ar1)`, so it does not persist.
- **Where statistics are weaker.** The gap is larger before 2000, in Sub-Saharan Africa and the Middle East, in the poorest countries, and in conflict and outlier years. In a regression of the absolute gap, outlier years add `r sprintf("%.1f", gr$abs_gap_model["outlier_5TRUE", 1])` pp and years after 2000 `r sprintf("%+.1f", gr$abs_gap_model["I(year >= 2000)TRUE", 1])` pp; income adds nothing (p = `r pv(gr$abs_gap_model["inc_level_wb", 4])`) once those are controlled.
- **A few countries drift**, with PWT growing persistently faster or slower than WB: `r paste(sprintf("%s (%+.1f pp a year)", name_of(gr$drift$GID_0[1:5]), gr$drift$mean[1:5]), collapse = ", ")`.
- **The gap does not follow the weather.** Regressed on the four weather arms with the handout's fixed effects and trends, it gives p = `r pv(src$weather$p_gap)` jointly. The warm arm is `r sprintf("%+.2f", src$weather$coef["pTM", "PWT"])` pp per SD with PWT growth and `r sprintf("%+.2f", src$weather$coef["pTM", "WB"])` with WB growth. The gap is noise in the outcome: it widens the SEs but does not bias the weather coefficients.

**How the two sources differ: income levels.** Here PPP against exchange rates matters, and systematically (the Penn effect).

**Table 17. Trailing income by WB income quintile: WB (2015 US\$, exchange rates), PWT (2021 PPP US\$), and their ratio.**

```{r table17}
q <- lv$quintile
autofit(bold(flextable(data.frame(Quintile = paste0("Q", q$quintile), `WB (US$)` = format(round(q$mer, -1), big.mark = ","),
                                  `PWT (PPP US$)` = format(round(q$ppp, -1), big.mark = ","),
                                  `PPP / WB` = sprintf("%.2f", q$ratio), check.names = FALSE)), part = "header"))
```

The log ratio falls by `r sprintf("%.2f", -lv$slope)` per log point of WB income. Ranks barely change (Spearman `r sprintf("%.2f", lv$rank_cor)`), and the ratio hardly moves within a country (SD `r sprintf("%.2f", lv$sd_within)` within, `r sprintf("%.2f", lv$sd_between)` between). So log income is more spread out with WB data, which changes the scale of ξ: with a spread larger by a factor $k$, the same scaling has $1 - \xi$ smaller by $k$.

**ξ with World Bank GDP.** The sample has `r format(wbe$sample[["rows"]], big.mark = ",")` country-years and `r wbe$sample[["countries"]]` countries.

**Table 18. Nonlinear least-squares estimate of ξ with World Bank GDP: $\hat\xi$ = `r sprintf("%.2f", wbe$xi_nls$estimate)` (Wald SE `r sprintf("%.2f", wbe$xi_nls$wald[["se"]])`, bootstrap SE `r sprintf("%.2f", wbe$xi_nls$boot[["se"]])`).**

```{r table18}
autofit(bold(flextable(xi_table(wbe, pv)), part = "header"))
```

```{r fig-xi-wb, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5.4, fig.cap = "As the figure of Section 6, with World Bank GDP. Dashed line: the estimate; grey lines: ξ = 0, 0.6 and 1."}
xi_figure(wbe)
```

**Same rows, different source.** The two samples differ: `r format(e$sample[["rows"]] - pce$sample[["rows"]], big.mark = ",")` PWT rows have no WB data, and WB covers more countries. To isolate the source, both are re-estimated on the `r format(pce$sample[["rows"]], big.mark = ",")` rows they share (`r pce$sample[["countries"]]` countries). There the weather, climate, share, controls and trends are identical; only the growth outcome and the trailing income differ. The two bootstraps use the same country draws, so the difference in ξ can be bootstrapped draw by draw.

**Table 19. ξ by GDP source and sample. p-values: Wald / robust test / bootstrap.**

```{r table19}
runs <- list(`PWT, own rows` = e, `PWT, common rows` = pce, `WB, common rows` = wce, `WB, own rows` = wbe)
autofit(bold(flextable(xi_compare_table(runs, pv)), part = "header"))
```

```{r fig-xi-common, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5.4, fig.cap = "PWT and World Bank GDP on the same rows. Top: profiles of the fit; middle: bootstrap estimates (the same country draws for both); bottom: the difference in ξ, draw by draw. Dashed lines: the estimates."}
xi_compare_figure(pce, wce, c("PWT", "WB"))
```

**Table 20. ξ on the common rows with the outcome and the income of the scaling taken from either source.**

```{r table20}
autofit(bold(flextable(data.frame(Outcome = sub(",.*", "", names(sw$xi)), `Income in the scaling` = sub(".*, ", "", names(sw$xi)),
                                  `ξ̂` = sprintf("%.2f", sw$xi), `Change from PWT` = sprintf("%+.2f", sw$xi - sw$xi[[1]]),
                                  check.names = FALSE)), part = "header"))
```

**Result.**

- **The picture is the same with WB data.** ξ is weakly identified (bootstrap SE `r sprintf("%.2f", wbe$xi_nls$boot[["se"]])`), ξ = 0 is never rejected, and ξ = 1 is rejected by the Wald test with both sources, and at the margin by the robust test. ξ = 0.6 is rejected with PWT, not with WB.
- **The source, not the sample, moves the estimate.** On the same rows, $\hat\xi$ is `r sprintf("%.2f", pce$xi_nls$estimate)` with PWT and `r sprintf("%.2f", wce$xi_nls$estimate)` with WB. Changing the sample moves it by only `r sprintf("%+.2f", pce$xi_nls$estimate - e$xi_nls$estimate)` (PWT) and `r sprintf("%+.2f", wbe$xi_nls$estimate - wce$xi_nls$estimate)` (WB).
- **Half outcome, half income.** WB growth alone moves ξ by `r sprintf("%+.2f", sw$xi[[2]] - sw$xi[[1]])`, WB income alone by `r sprintf("%+.2f", sw$xi[[3]] - sw$xi[[1]])`, and together by `r sprintf("%+.2f", sw$xi[[4]] - sw$xi[[1]])`. WB log income is `r sprintf("%.2f", sw$income_spread)` times as spread out as PWT's on these rows, which alone would move ξ by about `r sprintf("%+.2f", (1 - sw$xi[[1]]) * (1 - 1 / sw$income_spread))`. The rest comes from which countries are richer under each source.
- **The difference is not significant.** The paired bootstrap gives `r sprintf("%+.2f", wce$xi_nls$estimate - pce$xi_nls$estimate)` with SE `r sprintf("%.2f", sd(dx))` (95% `r sprintf("[%.1f, %.1f]", quantile(dx, 0.025), quantile(dx, 0.975))`, p = `r pv(min(1, 2 * min(mean(dx <= 0), mean(dx >= 0))))`). The draws correlate at only `r sprintf("%.2f", cor(pce$xi_nls$boot_draws, wce$xi_nls$boot_draws))` across sources: in the same resample, the two sources pull ξ to different places, as expected when it is weakly identified.
- **The income dependence itself is clearer with PWT.** The T × income interaction of M2 has p = `r pv(e$tests$interactions["T income", "p"])` with PWT and `r pv(wbe$tests$interactions["T income", "p"])` with WB (`r pv(pce$tests$interactions["T income", "p"])` and `r pv(wce$tests$interactions["T income", "p"])` on the common rows).

# 13. Methods: the tests of ξ and the bootstrap

Every test of ξ = ξ₀ starts from the same step: with ξ fixed at ξ₀, the model is linear and is estimated by the usual fixed-effects regression. The tests differ in what they add to it.

**Score test (C(α); Table 5, orange dashed line in the figures).** It adds one regressor, the derivative of the fitted temperature part in ξ, $h_{it} = y_{it}\, (\bar Y / Y_{it})^{1-\xi_0} \hat f_T$, and tests its coefficient with a clustered t. It asks whether moving ξ slightly away from ξ₀ would improve the fit: it tests the *slope* of the profile.

- It does not reject wherever the slope is zero, at maxima of the profile as well as at its minimum (with PWT near ξ = 2.5, where the fit is about 50 AIC points worse than at $\hat\xi$).
- $h$ contains the estimated response $\hat f_T$. Where the response is small, $h$ carries little information and the test's distribution is unreliable.

**Robust test (Anderson–Rubin type; blue line).** It adds $y_{it}$ times each of the four scaled temperature terms (warm, cold, and each times the climate) as free regressors, and tests them jointly with a clustered F. It asks whether any income gradient is left in the temperature response after scaling it with ξ₀.

- If ξ₀ is true, these terms are exactly zero whatever the size of the temperature response, so the test keeps its size where the response is small (the analogue of the Anderson–Rubin test with weak instruments).
- It has less power: four restrictions instead of one. Far from ξ = 1 it has none, because the scaling puts almost all the weight on a few of the poorest (ξ ≪ 0) or richest (ξ ≫ 1) countries, where $y$ barely varies. Its p-value near 1 at ξ = −4 says that the test cannot see anything there, not that ξ = −4 fits: the profile is 40 AIC points worse.

**Wald test.** The clustered covariance of the full nonlinear model (from the Gauss–Newton regression at $\hat\xi$). It is valid when ξ is well identified, which here it is not, so its interval is too narrow.

**Country bootstrap.** A nonparametric pairs bootstrap by cluster:

- `r e$xi_nls$boot[["reps"]]` replications; each draws `r e$sample[["countries"]]` countries with replacement and keeps all the years of each, preserving the serial correlation within countries;
- a country drawn more than once enters as separate countries, each with its own fixed effect and trends;
- in each replication ξ is re-estimated by profile NLS as in the main estimate (a grid over [−4, 4] in steps of 0.5, then a continuous search), so the fixed effects, trends and all other coefficients are re-estimated too;
- SE = SD of the estimates; 95% interval = 2.5–97.5% percentiles; p-value of ξ₀ = twice the smaller share of estimates on either side of ξ₀;
- the same seed and countries give the same draws for PWT and WB on the common rows, so their difference is a paired bootstrap.

Its limits come from the weak identification: the percentile interval of a weakly identified estimator has no guaranteed coverage, and estimates beyond the search bounds are stacked at ±4, so the lower end of its interval is "−4 or below".

**Would a sign change with income bias the tests?** The scaled form cannot change sign with income: every country loses from a warm year, less if richer. If the truth were the linear income interaction of M2b, where rich countries gain (Section 5), the scaled model would be misspecified. A Monte Carlo checks what the procedure does then. Samples are generated from the fitted M2b (its fitted values plus its residuals times a random sign per country), and ξ is estimated and tested in each. As a check of size, samples are also generated from the scaled model with ξ = 0.6, where the robust test of ξ = 0.6 should reject 5% of the time.

```{r mc-numbers, include = FALSE}
mc <- readRDS(file.path(base_dir, "xi_montecarlo.rds"))
mcs <- function(k) {
  x <- mc[[k]]
  data.frame(`Data generated by` = k, Samples = nrow(x),
             `ξ̂: median [IQR]` = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", median(x[, "xi"]), quantile(x[, "xi"], 0.25),
                                       quantile(x[, "xi"], 0.75)),
             `At −4` = pct(mean(x[, "xi"] <= -4)),
             `Rejects ξ = 0` = pct(mean(x[, "p0"] < 0.05)), `Rejects ξ = 0.6` = pct(mean(x[, "p06"] < 0.05)),
             `Rejects ξ = 1` = pct(mean(x[, "p1"] < 0.05)), check.names = FALSE)
}
mc_tab <- rbind(mcs("M2b"), mcs("scaled_0.6"))
mc_tab$`Data generated by` <- c("M2b: linear income (rich countries gain)", "Scaled model, ξ = 0.6")
```

**Table 21. Monte Carlo: estimate of ξ and rejection rates of the robust test at 5%.**

```{r table21}
autofit(bold(flextable(mc_tab), part = "header"))
```

```{r mc-get, include = FALSE}
mm <- function(k, col) mean(mc[[k]][, col] < 0.05)
```

**Result. A sign change does not push ξ to an extreme, but the tests reject too often even when the model is right.**

- **With rich countries gaining (M2b)**, the scaled model cannot reproduce the gain. The best it can do is a response that falls steeply with income, and $\hat\xi$ settles near equal dollars (median `r sprintf("%.2f", median(mc$M2b[, "xi"]))`), not at an extreme. The robust test rejects every value more often (`r pct(mm("M2b", "p0"))`, `r pct(mm("M2b", "p06"))` and `r pct(mm("M2b", "p1"))` for ξ = 0, 0.6 and 1): it partly detects the misspecification. With the data, ξ = 0 is not rejected, which argues weakly against a strong sign change; Section 7 finds the two forms indifferent in fit.
- **Size.** When the scaled model with ξ = 0.6 is true, the robust test rejects ξ = 0.6 in `r pct(mm("scaled_0.6", "p06"))` of the samples, not 5%. Clustered tests over-reject when a few clusters dominate a regressor, and the scaled terms put much of their weight on the poorest countries. The test is robust to a small response, not to this. Its p-values, and the Wald ones, which rely on the same clustered covariance, are therefore too small. "Rejected at 5%" in Tables 5b, 18 and 19 means less than it says, and the rejection of ξ = 0.6 with PWT is weaker evidence than its p-value suggests.
- **Bias.** In the same samples $\hat\xi$ has median `r sprintf("%.2f", median(mc$scaled_0.6[, "xi"]))` against a true 0.6: the estimator is biased downward, as the long left tail of the bootstrap suggests. The estimates with the data, `r sprintf("%.2f", e$xi_nls$estimate)` (PWT) and `r sprintf("%.2f", wbe$xi_nls$estimate)` (WB), are compatible with somewhat higher true values.

A wild cluster bootstrap of the robust test with the null imposed would correct its size. Section 14 applies it to the tests of the coefficients; for the test of ξ it has not been run yet.

# 14. Robust inference: few effective clusters and cross-country correlation

```{r robust-setup, include = FALSE}
inf <- readRDS(file.path(base_dir, "inference.rds"))
infr <- inf$results
main_key <- "PWT ERA5"
methods <- c("CR1", "WCR", "CR3", "2-way", "DK", paste0("Conley ", inf$cutoffs, " km"))
TEST_LABELS <- c(`T terms` = "All T terms", `P terms` = "All P terms", `warm arm` = "Warm arm, all its terms",
                 `cold arm` = "Cold arm, all its terms", `wet arm` = "Wet arm, all its terms", `dry arm` = "Dry arm, all its terms",
                 `T x climate` = "T × climate, both arms", `T x income` = "T × income, both arms",
                 `P x climate` = "P × climate, both arms", `P x share` = "P × share, both arms")
test_label <- function(x) ifelse(x %in% names(TEST_LABELS), TEST_LABELS[x], trimws(TERM_LABELS[x]))
p_of <- function(r, mod, test, k) r[[mod]]$p[[k]][r[[mod]]$p$test == test]
n_sig <- function(mod, test, k) sum(vapply(infr, function(r) p_of(r, mod, test, k) < 0.05, TRUE))
rng <- function(x, d = 0) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f–%.", d, "f"), min(x), max(x))
gstar <- function(mod, term) sapply(infr, function(r) r[[mod]]$coef$gstar[r[[mod]]$coef$term == term])
se_ratio <- function(mod, k) apply(sapply(infr, function(r) r[[mod]]$coef[[k]] / r[[mod]]$coef$CR1), 1, median)
G_main <- infr[[main_key]]$Pref$G
```

Every p-value so far comes from errors clustered by country (CR1), tested against F(q, G − 1). Two features of this panel can make those p-values too small.

- **Few effective clusters.** Clustered tests assume that many countries each contribute a little. When a coefficient is identified by a handful of countries, the clustered variance is too small and the tests over-reject. In Section 13, the robust test of ξ rejected a true value in `r pct(mm("scaled_0.6", "p06"))` of the samples.
- **Correlation across countries.** Year effects remove the shock common to all countries in a year. They do not remove correlation among neighbours (a regional drought), nor a common shock to which countries respond differently. Country clusters ignore both.

The preferred specification (ξ = 0) and M2b are therefore re-tested on all six datasets: PWT and WB GDP × ERA5, CRU TS and UDel weather. Each dataset keeps its own sample and the outlier rule of Section 1; with WB GDP and ERA5 the sample is that of Section 12. The alternatives are:

- **WCR**, a wild cluster restricted bootstrap by country. The null is imposed, the residuals of each country are multiplied by one random Webb weight, and the CR1 Wald statistic is recomputed in each of `r format(inf$B, big.mark = ",")` draws. It is the standard fix for few or unbalanced clusters (MacKinnon, Nielsen and Webb 2023).
- **CR3**, the jackknife variance: the coefficients re-estimated without each country in turn (exactly, not approximated).
- **2-way**, errors clustered by country and by year.
- **DK**, Driscoll–Kraay errors. They allow any correlation across countries within a year, and serial correlation of the yearly averages.
- **Conley**, country clusters plus spatial correlation between countries in the same year (Conley–Hsiang). The weight of a pair falls linearly with the distance between the countries' centroids, reaching zero at `r paste(format(inf$cutoffs, big.mark = ","), collapse = ", ")` km.
- **G\***, the effective number of clusters of each coefficient (Carter, Schnepel and Steigerwald 2017). It measures how unevenly the countries share the coefficient's leverage, and equals the number of countries when all weigh the same.

All are computed on the model's own design: country effects and trends partialled out, year effects as dummies. CR1 reproduces the p-values of the previous sections.

**Table 22. p-values by method, PWT × ERA5; in brackets, the number of the six datasets with p < 0.05.**

```{r table22}
p_rows <- function(mod, tests) {
  out <- data.frame(Model = mod, Test = unname(test_label(tests)), check.names = FALSE)
  for (k in methods) out[[sub(" km", "", k)]] <- vapply(tests, function(t) sprintf("%s (%d)", pv(p_of(infr[[main_key]], mod, t, k)), n_sig(mod, t, k)), "")
  out
}
tab <- rbind(
  p_rows("Pref", c("pTM:r", "pTM:clim_TM:r", "nTM:r", "pRR", "nRR", "nRR:clim_RR", "nRR:agr", "T terms", "warm arm", "cold arm",
                   "P terms", "wet arm", "dry arm", "P x climate", "P x share")),
  p_rows("M2b", c("pTM", "pTM:y", "pTM:clim_TM", "nTM:y", "warm arm", "T x income", "T x climate", "T terms")))
ft <- merge_v(flextable(tab), j = "Model")
ft <- valign(ft, j = 1, valign = "top")
ft <- hline(ft, i = 15, border = officer::fp_border(width = 0.75))
autofit(bold(ft, part = "header"))
```

**Table 23. Effective number of clusters G\* and largest partial leverage (PWT × ERA5; ISO codes, share of the coefficient's leverage), and the SE of each method relative to CR1 (median over the six datasets).**

```{r table23}
lev_rows <- function(mod, terms) {
  cf <- infr[[main_key]][[mod]]$coef
  i <- match(terms, cf$term)
  g_all <- t(sapply(terms, function(t) gstar(mod, t)))
  ratio <- function(k) sprintf("%.2f", se_ratio(mod, k)[i])
  data.frame(Model = mod, Coefficient = unname(trimws(TERM_LABELS[terms])), `G*` = round(cf$gstar[i]),
             `G*, six datasets` = sprintf("%.0f–%.0f", apply(g_all, 1, min), apply(g_all, 1, max)),
             CR3 = ratio("CR3"), `2-way` = ratio("2-way"), DK = ratio("DK"), `Conley 2000` = ratio("Conley 2000 km"),
             `Largest leverage` = vapply(strsplit(cf$top_leverage[i], ", "), function(x) paste(x[1:3], collapse = ", "), ""),
             check.names = FALSE)
}
pref_terms <- infr[[main_key]]$Pref$coef$term
tab <- rbind(lev_rows("Pref", pref_terms), lev_rows("M2b", grep("TM", infr[[main_key]]$M2b$coef$term, value = TRUE)))
ft <- merge_v(flextable(tab), j = "Model")
ft <- valign(ft, j = 1, valign = "top")
ft <- hline(ft, i = length(pref_terms), border = officer::fp_border(width = 0.75))
autofit(bold(ft, part = "header"))
```

**Result. Drought survives every method; the warm-year response survives too, but it rests on few countries and is the most sensitive to correlation across countries.**

- **Drought is robust.** The dry arm and dry × share have p < 0.05 in all six datasets under every method, and so do the P terms jointly. P × climate is the only P result that two-way clustering weakens (`r n_sig("Pref", "P x climate", "2-way")` of 6).
- **The warm arm survives, but its identification is thin.** The warm arm of the preferred specification is significant in `r n_sig("Pref", "pTM:r", "WCR")` of 6 datasets with the bootstrap and `r n_sig("Pref", "pTM:r", "CR3")` with CR3. But its G\* is only `r rng(gstar("Pref", "pTM:r"))` out of about `r G_main` countries, and `r rng(gstar("Pref", "nTM:clim_TM:r"))` for the cold × climate term. The scaling Ȳ/Y gives the poorest countries the largest values of the T terms, so a few of them (Mozambique, Lesotho, Malawi, Mali, China, Myanmar) carry 6–23% of a coefficient's leverage each. This is the situation in which CR1 over-rejects. The joint test of the four T terms shows it most: with PWT × ERA5, p = `r pv(p_of(infr[[main_key]], "Pref", "T terms", "CR1"))` with CR1 against `r pv(p_of(infr[[main_key]], "Pref", "T terms", "WCR"))` with the bootstrap. In M2b, where income enters linearly, the T terms have G\* of `r rng(c(gstar("M2b", "pTM"), gstar("M2b", "pTM:y")))`.
- **Correlation across countries matters for warm years, not for precipitation.** Conley errors are at most about 10% larger than CR1, so correlation among neighbours adds little. Two-way and Driscoll–Kraay errors are up to `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (max(se_ratio("Pref", "2-way")[1:2]) - 1))`% larger on the warm terms of the preferred specification. That points to shocks common to a year to which countries respond differently, which the year effects do not absorb. With these errors, M2b's warm arm is significant in only `r n_sig("M2b", "warm arm", "2-way")` (two-way) and `r n_sig("M2b", "warm arm", "DK")` (DK) of 6 datasets. Its income gradient holds better: `r n_sig("M2b", "T x income", "2-way")` and `r n_sig("M2b", "T x income", "DK")` of 6.
- **No single country dominates.** CR3 errors are within `r sprintf("%.0f", 100 * (max(se_ratio("Pref", "CR3"), se_ratio("M2b", "CR3")) - 1))`% of CR1, mostly on the cold terms. The fragility is that few countries carry the warm response, not that one outlier does. Section 15 measures it.
- **The cold arm and wet arm stay insignificant**, or significant in one dataset only, under every method.

# 15. Influence: which countries drive the warm and dry responses

```{r influence-setup, include = FALSE}
ifl <- readRDS(file.path(base_dir, "influence.rds"))
ir <- ifl$results
TARGET_LABELS <- c(`Pref warm arm` = "Warm arm (Pref)", `Pref dry arm` = "Dry arm (Pref)", `Pref dry x share` = "Dry × share (Pref)",
                   `M2b warm x income` = "Warm × income (M2b)", `M2b warm x climate` = "Warm × climate (M2b)",
                   `Income only: warm x income` = "Warm × income, no climate interaction",
                   `Climate only: warm x climate` = "Warm × climate, no income interaction")
k_of <- function(s, what) vapply(ir, function(r) r$minimal[[s]][[what]], 0)
first_drops <- function(s, n = 8) {
  f <- sort(table(unlist(lapply(ir, function(r) head(r$minimal[[s]]$path$dropped[-1], n)))), decreasing = TRUE)
  f[f >= 3]
}
recurring <- function(s) paste(sprintf("%s (%d)", name_of(names(first_drops(s))), first_drops(s)), collapse = ", ")
loo_top <- function(s, n = 5) {
  x <- head(ir[[main_key]]$influence[[s]], n)
  paste(sprintf("%s %+.2f", name_of(x$GID_0), x$change_se), collapse = ", ")
}
full <- function(d, s) ir[[d]]$minimal[[s]]$path[1, ]
```

Section 14 shows that the warm response rests on few countries. This section asks which countries, how many of them, and whether the warm response depends on income or on the long-run temperature. Same models, datasets and errors as Section 14 (CR1, which the bootstrap broadly confirmed).

- **Leave one country out.** Each country's exact effect on a coefficient: the change in the estimate when it is dropped, in SE of the full sample.
- **Minimal sets.** The country whose removal moves the coefficient most towards zero is dropped, the model is re-estimated, and the step is repeated. The table reports how many countries had been dropped when the coefficient stopped being significant at 5%, and when its sign flipped. The search is greedy, so the true minimum may be smaller. For warm × climate in M2b, which is not significant, the search goes the other way: it drops the countries that hold it back from a loss in hotter climates, until it becomes significant.

**Table 24. Minimal sets: countries dropped until p ≥ 0.05 / until the sign flips (out of about `r G_main` countries). Warm × climate in M2b: countries dropped until it becomes a significant loss in hotter climates.**

```{r table24}
cell <- function(m) {
  if (!is.na(m$k_significant) || all(is.na(c(m$k_insignificant, m$k_flip)))) {
    return(if (is.na(m$k_significant)) sprintf("not in %d", ifl$steps) else as.character(m$k_significant))
  }
  sprintf("%s / %s", m$k_insignificant, if (is.na(m$k_flip)) sprintf(">%d", ifl$steps) else m$k_flip)
}
tab <- data.frame(Coefficient = unname(TARGET_LABELS[names(ir[[1]]$minimal)]),
                  `PWT × ERA5: estimate (p)` = vapply(names(ir[[1]]$minimal), function(s) {
                    f <- full(main_key, s)
                    sprintf("%+.3f (%s)", 100 * f$est, pv(f$p))
                  }, ""),
                  t(sapply(names(ir[[1]]$minimal), function(s) vapply(ir, function(r) cell(r$minimal[[s]]), ""))),
                  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
autofit(bold(flextable(tab), part = "header"))
```

Estimates are in pp of growth per SD, and the interactions per log point of income or per °C.

**Table 25. The countries that matter: those among the first eight dropped in at least three of the six datasets (number of datasets), and the largest leave-one-out changes with PWT × ERA5 (in SE; positive: the country makes the estimate more negative, i.e. the loss larger or the income gradient smaller).**

```{r table25}
keys <- c(`Pref warm arm` = "Pref pTM_X_r", `Pref dry arm` = "Pref nRR", `Pref dry x share` = "Pref nRR_X_agr",
          `M2b warm x income` = "M2b pTM_X_y")
tab <- data.frame(Coefficient = unname(TARGET_LABELS[names(keys)]),
                  `Recurring in the minimal sets` = vapply(names(keys), recurring, ""),
                  `Largest leave-one-out changes, PWT × ERA5` = vapply(keys, loo_top, ""),
                  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
ft <- flextable(tab)
ft <- width(ft, j = 1, width = 1.2)
ft <- width(ft, j = 2:3, width = 2.7)
bold(ft, part = "header")
```

```{r fig-influence, fig.width = 6.8, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Leave-one-out change of the warm arm and the dry arm of the preferred specification, PWT × ERA5, in SE of the full-sample estimate, against the country's mean income. Positive: dropping the country moves the estimate towards zero (the country makes the loss larger). Colour: mean temperature. Labels: the eight largest changes."}
fig_dat <- rbind(cbind(ir[[main_key]]$influence[["Pref pTM_X_r"]], arm = "Warm arm"),
                 cbind(ir[[main_key]]$influence[["Pref nRR"]], arm = "Dry arm"))
fig_dat$arm <- factor(fig_dat$arm, c("Warm arm", "Dry arm"))
fig_dat$label <- ""
for (a in levels(fig_dat$arm)) {
  i <- which(fig_dat$arm == a)
  top <- i[order(-abs(fig_dat$change_se[i]))][1:8]
  fig_dat$label[top] <- fig_dat$GID_0[top]
}
ggplot(fig_dat, aes(income, change_se)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(fill = temp), shape = 21, colour = "grey35", size = 1.8, stroke = 0.25) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = label), size = 2.3, colour = "grey20", min.segment.length = 0, segment.size = 0.2,
                           seed = 1) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2b6cb0", mid = "white", high = "#c53030", midpoint = 15, name = "Mean T (°C)") +
  facet_wrap(~arm) +
  labs(x = "Mean income (2021 PPP US$, log scale)", y = "Change when dropped (SE)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 8) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.key.height = unit(0.4, "cm"))
```

**Result: which countries.**

- **Warm years: mostly poor countries of southern and east Africa.** The warm arm loses significance after `r rng(k_of("Pref warm arm", "k_insignificant"))` countries and flips after `r rng(k_of("Pref warm arm", "k_flip"))`. Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Morocco are among the first dropped in every dataset; Lesotho, Nepal, China and Peru follow. Mozambique alone moves the estimate by `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(ir[[main_key]]$influence[["Pref pTM_X_r"]]$change_se[1]))` SE with PWT × ERA5, and with WB × ERA5 dropping it is enough to lose significance. Rwanda and Myanmar pull the other way: dropping them makes the loss larger.
- **Dry years: the Sahel, plus Syria.** The dry arm needs `r rng(k_of("Pref dry arm", "k_insignificant"))` countries to lose significance and `r rng(k_of("Pref dry arm", "k_flip"))` to flip, the most of any result. Niger, Guinea-Bissau and Syria are among the first dropped in every dataset, then Mozambique, Mauritania, Malawi and Sudan. Dry × share depends on the same countries and is less robust (`r rng(k_of("Pref dry x share", "k_insignificant"))` / `r rng(k_of("Pref dry x share", "k_flip"))`). Syria is the odd one: its income differs about tenfold between PWT (about \$12,000) and WB (about \$1,000), and its rows deserve a check before much is read into its weight.
- **How fragile is this?** Losing significance after dropping a handful of `r G_main` countries is fragile by the usual standard (Broderick, Giordano and Meager 2023). Here that happens after `r min(k_of("Pref warm arm", "k_insignificant"))`–`r max(k_of("Pref dry arm", "k_insignificant"))` countries for the warm and dry arms. The sign is much harder to move: `r min(k_of("Pref warm arm", "k_flip"))` or more countries for the warm arm and `r min(k_of("Pref dry arm", "k_flip"))` or more for the dry arm. The direction of both responses is solid; their size and precision depend on a small group of poor countries.

**Income or the long-run temperature?** The two are related but far from collinear: across countries, log income and mean temperature correlate at between `r sprintf("%.2f", min(vapply(ir, function(r) r$cor_income_temp, 0)))` and `r sprintf("%.2f", max(vapply(ir, function(r) r$cor_income_temp, 0)))`. Their roles in the warm response are compared in three ways:

- each alone, with the warm and cold arms interacted with income only or with climate only;
- both together (M2b);
- M2b without the countries that separate the two. These are the `r ifl$n_separate` countries richest for their climate and the `r ifl$n_separate` poorest for theirs: the largest and smallest residuals of mean log income regressed on mean temperature.

With PWT × ERA5, the richest for their climate are `r paste(name_of(ir[[main_key]]$separate[[1]]), collapse = ", ")`. The poorest are `r paste(name_of(ir[[main_key]]$separate[[2]]), collapse = ", ")`.

**Table 26. Income against climate as the moderator of the warm response: estimate (pp per SD per log point of income, or per °C) and p, by dataset.**

```{r table26}
est_p <- function(est, p, d) sprintf(paste0("%+.", d, "f (%s)"), 100 * est, pv(p))
model_rows <- function(s, lab, d) vapply(ir, function(r) { f <- r$minimal[[s]]$path[1, ]; est_p(f$est, f$p, d) }, "")
race_rows <- function(row, v, d) vapply(ir, function(r) est_p(r$race[row, paste0(v, "_est")], r$race[row, paste0(v, "_p")], d), "")
tab <- rbind(
  c("Income only", "warm × income", model_rows("Income only: warm x income", "", 2)),
  c("Climate only", "warm × climate", model_rows("Climate only: warm x climate", "", 3)),
  c("Both (M2b)", "warm × income", race_rows("none", "income", 2)),
  c("Both (M2b)", "warm × climate", race_rows("none", "climate", 3)),
  c("M2b without the rich for their climate", "warm × income", race_rows("rich for their climate", "income", 2)),
  c("M2b without the rich for their climate", "warm × climate", race_rows("rich for their climate", "climate", 3)),
  c("M2b without the poor for their climate", "warm × income", race_rows("poor for their climate", "income", 2)),
  c("M2b without the poor for their climate", "warm × climate", race_rows("poor for their climate", "climate", 3)),
  c("M2b without both", "warm × income", race_rows("both", "income", 2)),
  c("M2b without both", "warm × climate", race_rows("both", "climate", 3)))
tab <- as.data.frame(tab, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(tab) <- c("Model", "Gradient", names(ir))
ft <- merge_v(flextable(tab), j = "Model")
ft <- valign(ft, j = 1, valign = "top")
autofit(bold(ft, part = "header"))
```

```{r race-numbers, include = FALSE}
inc_sig <- function(row) sum(vapply(ir, function(r) r$race[row, "income_p"] < 0.05, TRUE))
clim_loss <- function(row) sum(vapply(ir, function(r) r$race[row, "climate_p"] < 0.05 && r$race[row, "climate_est"] < 0, TRUE))
alone <- function(s) vapply(ir, function(r) r$minimal[[s]]$path$p[1], 0)
```

**Result: income, not the long-run temperature, moderates the warm response.**

- **Alone, climate does nothing.** With climate as the only moderator, the warm × climate gradient is significant in `r sum(alone("Climate only: warm x climate") < 0.05)` of 6 datasets. Where it is (WB × UDel), dropping `r max(k_of("Climate only: warm x climate", "k_insignificant"))` countries removes it. Income alone is significant in `r sum(alone("Income only: warm x income") < 0.05)` of 6 (p `r rng(alone("Income only: warm x income"), 3)`).
- **Together, income wins.** In M2b the income gradient is significant in `r inc_sig("none")` of 6 datasets. The climate gradient is never a significant loss in hotter climates, and its sign is that of a smaller loss in hotter climates in `r sum(vapply(ir, function(r) r$race["none", "climate_est"] > 0, TRUE))` of 6.
- **Not an artefact of a few unusual countries.** Without the rich-for-their-climate countries (mostly Gulf states, Singapore and small islands), the income gradient is significant in `r inc_sig("rich for their climate")` of 6 and usually larger. Without the poor-for-their-climate countries (Lesotho, Mongolia, the Central Asian and Himalayan states…), in `r inc_sig("poor for their climate")` of 6. Without both, in `r inc_sig("both")` of 6. Climate becomes a significant loss moderator in none of these samples.
- **The significance of the income gradient is fragile, its sign is not.** In M2b it loses significance after `r rng(k_of("M2b warm x income", "k_insignificant"))` countries (Mozambique, Burkina Faso, Morocco, Mali, Zimbabwe, and Saudi Arabia among the rich), but needs `r rng(k_of("M2b warm x income", "k_flip"))` to flip. Making climate a significant loss moderator takes the removal of `r rng(k_of("M2b warm x climate", "k_significant"))` countries chosen for that purpose, comparable to what it takes to flip income. On this measure alone the comparison favours income only moderately. The stronger evidence is the previous two points: climate is null on its own and in every subsample.

**What to take from Sections 14–15.**

- The drought loss and its share gradient are the most robust results: significant under every error and every dataset, and the hardest to overturn by dropping countries.
- The warm-year loss is moderated by income, not by the long-run temperature, in every dataset and every subsample tried.
- The size and significance of the warm loss rest on a small group of poor southern- and east-African countries, roughly 10–25 effective clusters. Its bootstrap p-values (Table 22) are the ones to quote.

# Notes

- Sources: estimates from `handout_preferred_specification.R` (saved to `results/handout_preferred_specification/estimates.rds`), on the panel of the response explorer (`apps/response_explorer/build_models.R`). Projections from `handout_projections.R` (`projections.rds`), using the explorer's projection code and scenario data (`apps/response_explorer/build_scenarios.R`). This document: `handout_preferred_specification.Rmd`.
- Section 12: the same script with `HANDOUT_GDP=WB` (folder `WB`) and with `HANDOUT_ROWS=common` for each source (folders `PWT_common`, `WB_common`); the comparison of the two sources in `handout_sources.R` (`sources.rds`). Section 13: `handout_xi_montecarlo.R` (`xi_montecarlo.rds`). The tables and figures of ξ: `handout_xi_figure.R`. The bootstraps are cached in `xi_bootstrap.rds` in each folder. Section 14: `handout_inference.R` (`inference.rds`). Section 15: `handout_influence.R` (`influence.rds`).
- The estimates with ξ = 0.6, the previous preferred value, are kept in `estimates_xi06.rds`, `app_models_xi06.rds` and `projections_xi06.rds`.
- All models use the same rows and include the level controls, so their fits are comparable.
- The deviations use the trailing mean but the long-run SD. The response explorer's 20-year baseline uses the trailing SD instead, so its coefficients differ slightly from these.
- Natural variability is an option of the response explorer's climate scenarios and termination shocks (none, independent years, joint years, joint 5-year blocks), with the noise pools built by `build_models.R`. The noise keeps its historical size under warming, and the pool has only `r e$horizon[2] - e$horizon[1] + 1` historical years, so the number of distinct global patterns is limited.
